value.overview: The Chestnut-colored Woodpecker (Celeus castaneus) is a medium-sized, mainly chestnut-brown woodpecker of humid forests in southern Mexico and Central America. It has a shaggy, pointed crest and a strongly contrasting pale, often buff-colored head. Males show red around the lores and behind the eye, while females lack this red facial marking. The species is associated especially with lowland rainforest and is a native resident of Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Chestnut-colored Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Celeus. It is currently treated as a single species, Celeus castaneus.
value.identification: This woodpecker is about 22–24 cm long, with predominantly rich chestnut or rufous-brown plumage, a pale tawny head, and a prominent pointed crest. The back and wings may appear darker and finely barred, while the underparts are generally warm brown. Adult males have red feathering around the lores and behind the eye, extending toward the throat; females normally lack this red. Its heavy, pale bill and slow, deliberate movements are useful field marks.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Veracruz in Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and into western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in humid Caribbean-slope and northern lowland forests, including areas around Sarapiquí, Tortuguero, and other forested sites in the northern and eastern lowlands. It uses mature and partly disturbed tropical rainforest, forest edges, second growth, and wooded habitats where large trees, dead limbs, and epiphyte-rich vegetation provide foraging and nesting opportunities.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout most or all of its range. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding records are available from several parts of Central America, including Costa Rica, where nesting activity has been reported mainly from February through May, with some records possibly extending into July. Both sexes excavate a nest cavity, usually in a tree or dead limb. Details of incubation, parental care, and fledging are poorly documented. As with other woodpeckers, suitable trees with decayed wood are important for nest construction and successful reproduction.
value.dietFeeding: The Chestnut-colored Woodpecker feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods found in wood, bark, and epiphytes, including ants, termites, beetle larvae, and related prey. It searches by climbing along trunks and larger branches, probing or chiseling into soft or decaying wood with its strong bill. Fruit and other plant material may occasionally supplement the diet, but animal prey appears to be the principal food.
value.behavior: It is generally encountered singly or in pairs and forages methodically on trunks, limbs, and large vines. The species may join mixed-species feeding groups, especially in forested habitats. Its flight is undulating, as in many woodpeckers, and its calls include nasal, descending notes and short repeated phrases. Drumming consists of a brief series of rapid taps. It can be inconspicuous despite its bold plumage, particularly in dense rainforest.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is believed to be decreasing, although it is not currently considered globally threatened.
